[A large language model]{.newthought} generates text one token at a time. Each step runs the whole network on one new token per request, so the GPU must read every weight from memory to do only a little arithmetic. This post shows why that makes decoding limited by memory bandwidth rather than compute, and why batching and KV-cache management matter so much to inference engines such as vLLM [@kwon2023].

## Attention and the KV cache

Each Transformer layer computes scaled dot-product attention [@vaswani2017]:

$$
\mathrm{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V.
$$ {#eq-attn}

During decoding, the keys and values of earlier tokens never change, so engines store them in a *KV cache* instead of recomputing them. For a model with $L$ layers and $n_{kv}$ key-value heads of dimension $d_h$, serving a batch of $b$ sequences of length $s$ with $p$ bytes per element, the cache needs

$$
M_{\mathrm{KV}} = 2 \cdot L \cdot n_{kv} \cdot d_h \cdot s \cdot b \cdot p \ \text{bytes},
$$ {#eq-kv}

where the factor 2 counts both keys and values.[^gqa]

[^gqa]: Grouped-query attention [@ainslie2023] shares each key-value head across several query heads, which shrinks $n_{kv}$, and the cache, by the same factor.

Take a 7B model with 32 layers and 32 heads of dimension 128 (the shape of Llama 2 7B), stored in FP16. @eq-kv gives 0.5 MiB per token, so a single 4,096-token sequence already needs 2 GiB (@lst-kv, @tbl-kv).

::: {#lst-kv}
```python
def kv_cache_bytes(layers, kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch,
                   bytes_per_elem=2):
    return 2 * layers * kv_heads * head_dim * seq_len * batch * bytes_per_elem

kv_cache_bytes(32, 32, 128, 4096, 1) / 2**30   # 2.0 GiB
```

The KV cache size from @eq-kv, in bytes.
:::

| Sequence length | $b = 1$ | $b = 8$ |
|:---------------:|:-------:|:-------:|
| 2,048           | 1 GiB   | 8 GiB   |
| 4,096           | 2 GiB   | 16 GiB  |
| 32,768          | 16 GiB  | 128 GiB |

: KV cache size from @eq-kv for the 7B shape above in FP16. {#tbl-kv}

## Why decoding is memory-bound

The *arithmetic intensity* $I$ of a kernel is the number of floating-point operations it performs per byte it moves. The roofline model [@williams2009] says that on a machine with peak compute $P$ and memory bandwidth $B$, the kernel can reach at most

$$
\text{attainable FLOP/s} = \min(P,\; I \cdot B).
$$ {#eq-roofline}

::: {#prp-intensity}
## Intensity of a decode step
Multiply a weight matrix $W \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ stored in FP16 by a batch of $b$ activation vectors. The arithmetic intensity satisfies $I \le b$ FLOP/byte, and $I \approx b$ when $b \ll \min(m, n)$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The product takes $2mnb$ FLOPs: one multiply and one add per weight per vector. It reads the $mn$ weights and the $bn$ inputs and writes the $bm$ outputs, at 2 bytes each, so
$$
I = \frac{2mnb}{2mn + 2b(m + n)} \le \frac{2mnb}{2mn} = b.
$$
When $b \ll \min(m, n)$, the term $2b(m + n)$ is small next to $2mn$, so $I \approx b$.
:::

So a single request decodes at about 1 FLOP per byte. NVIDIA's H100 SXM is specified at about 989 TFLOP/s of dense BF16 compute and 3.35 TB/s of memory bandwidth, a ratio of roughly 295 FLOP/byte.[^kv-reads] By @eq-roofline, the GPU stays bandwidth-limited until a batch holds about 295 sequences (@fig-roofline). That is why inference engines work so hard to batch requests together, and why the KV cache in @tbl-kv, which competes with the batch for GPU memory, is the resource they manage most carefully.

[^kv-reads]: This ignores reading the KV cache itself. That adds bytes at every step without adding weight FLOPs, so real decoding is even more memory-bound.
